A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Bongard Problems study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments with eight MLLMs across four BP datasets in Table 1, together with evaluator-validation and problem-coverage analyses in the appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original human-study, image-variant, concept-selection and model-scaling results in Section 5 and Appendices B–D.

M1.justification: V2 adds a constrained concept-selection procedure in which the model chooses among 2, 4, 8 or 16 supplied concepts. This is a limited input/output adaptation; the seven original generation strategies, four-model voting evaluator and Bongard-RWR generation algorithm remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The four underlying BP datasets are retained, but v2 adds a human-solving population and multiple-choice concept selection across all four datasets. These substantially extend population and task coverage. The grayscale and square-image RWR variants reuse existing problems rather than introducing new concepts.

E2.justification: V2 substantially expands the evaluated systems. Figure 10 adds GPT-4o mini, Gemini 1.5 Flash and larger InternVL2/LLaVA variants; Tables 2–3 include InternVL2.5 variants and Qwen2VL 72B-Instruct. Appendix B also supplies a human benchmark absent from v1.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a 30-participant open-ended study with manual adjudication, multiple-choice testing with varying candidate counts, and model-size comparisons using Direct and Descriptive strategies. New RWR preprocessing includes grayscale conversion and square cropping, with 512×512 panels and 1024×763 matrices. The original benchmark sample counts are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds color/cropping ablations, sensitivity to the number of candidate concepts, and model-scaling analyses in Appendices C–D. Appendix B examines human solvability, problem difficulty and human/model coverage. V1's evaluator-validation, strategy-overlap and synthetic-versus-real-world case analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V2 adds human-score variability reporting through a histogram and boxplot, mean/median/range summaries, and independent human-rater agreement reporting of 94.5% (Appendix B). Neither version reports repeated-model-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: All 320 entries in v1 Table 1 are retained in v2 Table 4. Substantial new results include human performance averaging 39.2/60, image-variant scores, concept-selection accuracies and scaling results. For example, Table 2 reports Phi-3.5-Vision solving 16 grayscale problems versus 1 under the original input condition. Figure 23 changes the aggregate RWR caption from 23 to 22, matching the unchanged plot, although Section 5 and Appendix G still state 23.

T1.justification: The BP formalization and dataset-generation mathematics are substantively unchanged, and neither version develops formal theorems or proofs. Newly specified candidate counts and negative-label indexing concern evaluation procedures rather than theoretical developments.

C1.justification: V2 removes the introduction's claim to consider BPs with MLLMs 'for the first time in the literature.' The main contributions and central claim that poor performance reflects broader reasoning limitations rather than synthetic imagery alone remain intact.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning color/layout sensitivity, structural versus surface-level recognition, the insufficiency of model scaling alone, and human evidence for dataset solvability. New Appendix A substantially discusses applicability beyond BPs, fine-grained perception and relationships to other AVR settings. These extend v1's explanations of model failures.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents stratified sampling from test splits, fixed negative-label selection with manual checking, image-resizing details and human-study instructions. These disclosures do not establish changes to the original samples. V2 explicitly announces code availability alongside data, while v1's prospective MIT-license statement disappears.

R1.justification: Section 2 replaces the assertion that MLLMs had not tackled BPs with explicit positioning against concurrent work by Wüst et al., emphasizing synthetic-versus-real-world comparisons. It also adds Perception Test and KiVA. Appendix A substantially expands connections to ConceptARC, VCog-Bench, MindSet: Vision and cognitive-assessment research.

P1.justification: V2 substantially condenses the abstract and reorganizes the narrative and appendices. Detailed binary-classification discussion moves from Section 5 to Appendix C, prompts move from Appendix A to Appendix I, and evaluation, dataset and coverage material are integrated into a new appendix structure.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, replaces examples in Figure 1, and redisplays original results through a compact generation table and new binary/strategy-effect plots. The complete original table moves to Appendix C. Human-study, concept-selection and scaling displays are added, while existing appendix graphics are largely retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked human validation of its new benchmark. V2's 30-person study establishes that every RWR problem was solved by at least one participant, addressing a central uncertainty about dataset solvability. Color/cropping controls and broader model comparisons also test alternative explanations for poor performance. The convenience sample, different human/model grading procedures and unresolved aggregate-count inconsistencies limit some comparisons, but the additions substantially strengthen the paper's empirical foundation.
